body: The Netherlands uses longyellow license plates with a European blue strip on the left; taxis have blue plates. Other European countries with yellow plates include Luxembourg and the UK, while older French and Danish coverage feature them on some vehicles.
Dutch is a Germanic language with distinctive letter clusters like ij, ieu, and oe. The capitalized “IJ” is unique and the language is also used in northern Belgium’s Flanders region.
The Netherlands features simple white bollards with red reflectors. Occasionally, round French-style bollards appear but with incomplete red wrapping compared to French ones.
Small street-level utility poles are rare in the Netherlands, though large power lines exist. In contrast, Belgium uses utility poles more frequently.
The Netherlands is remarkably flat and largely below sea level due to reclaimed land. Exceptions include low hills in southern Limburg and parts of the Veluwe region.
Waterways like canals and ditches are abundant. Water management infrastructure such as dikes, dams, and bridges is prominent.
Many rural roads are lined with rows of trees, a feature also common in Poland.
The country is known for its organized urban planning with well-maintained roads and master-planned suburbs featuring row houses.
Road lines are mostly white in the Netherlands, with common dashed sidelines and occasionally unique green center lines.
Dedicated bicycle paths flourish, often marked by a reddish-pink lane. Cycling is a very popular mode of transport.
Brick roads are widespread in both urban and rural settings.
Most sidewalks use grey square tiles with offset patterns; brick sidewalks may appear in historic areas.
Speed bumps are characterized by alternating long and short white stripes and appear on brick and asphalt roads.
Some rural roads have brick rumble strips along their sides, a uniquely Dutch feature.
Street signs are mostly blue with white lettering. Words like 'straat' and 'weg' are common for street names. 'Fietspad' signals bicycle paths.
Direction signs are blue with white text; cyclist signs are white with red borders.
Town entry signs are blue and sometimes very elaborate, often naming the municipality to aid location.
Road markers are green, with yellow boxes for regional (N) roads and red boxes for highways (A). Some have province-specific designs.
Dutch road signs have extended edges creating a visible border behind the sign, a design unique to the country.
Many signposts have striped markings in black-white or blue-white.
Bulky yellow signposts are commonly seen on traffic islands.
Some rural roads have distinctive striped road barriers.
Red-brown brick buildings with orange or gray roofs are common; similar styles also appear in Denmark and Belgium.
Row houses are prevalent in the Netherlands, forming nearly half the housing stock.
Traditional and modern windmills are common and iconic across the country.
Some Generation 4 Google Street View coverage may show glitches revealing the black back of the car.
The Netherlands has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage with a camera mounted lower and a large circular blur; this is common in Western Europe.
Landline phone numbers use geographically grouped three- or four-digit area codes; mobiles always start with 06.
Some regional road markers have province-specific designs for N-roads; A-roads are uniform and marked with red boxes; certain bollards show regional kilometre stickers.
Each Dutch province has a unique flag, though rarely seen; Friesland, Noord-Brabant, and the Achterhoek region are exceptions with more visibility.
Frisian is spoken in Friesland with bilingual town names and unique street name suffixes; its alphabet includes special vowels not found in Dutch.
Streetlights in Limburg feature long vertical white stickers with three to four digits.
North Brabant has streetlight stickers arranged horizontally with one or two digits.
Much of the west and north is low-lying or below sea level with marshy 'polder' landscapes and abundant waterways.
The south and east have typical flat European farmland with waterways but less marshiness.
Southern Limburg features some low hills, contrasting with the generally flat country.
The Veluwe area is forested with some elevation, old-growth forest, heath, or sandy soil; it may look unusual for the Netherlands.
Flevoland is mostly reclaimed land with man-made straight roads, large crop fields, and wind turbines; urban areas lack old buildings except the town of Urk.
The Dutch North Sea coast is lined with extensive dunes.
The Wadden Islands northwest are popular tourist spots with sandy coastlines and dunes.
Farms in the north frequently have very large roofs.
Rolling shutters are more common on houses in the south but can also appear in northern regions; use this clue cautiously.
Curaçao, north of Venezuela, is part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands and counted as the Netherlands for location purposes.
Amsterdam street signs include the district name below the street name, a feature rare in the rest of the country.
Buildings in the Zaanstreek near Amsterdam have wooden architectural elements in green or black with white trims and sometimes tall white roof spires.
The Afsluitdijk is a straight divided highway causeway between Noord-Holland and Friesland, distinguishable by water to the southeast and a dike to the northwest.
Westland municipality near The Hague is extensively covered by greenhouses.
In southern Veluwe’s National Park De Hoge Veluwe, a Google trekker is identifiable by the visible brown hair of the employee.
Rotterdam hosts one of the world’s largest harbors, with major industrial zones and large round fuel storage tanks.
Many Lelystad streets follow a naming pattern using neighborhood names followed by numbers, which appear on Google Maps.
Baarle is a southern Dutch village containing Belgian enclaves, evident through pavement markings and flying Dutch and Belgian flags.
